items.prompt: Sam's message asked Priya and Devon to be more respectful, and the clash returned. What was the message aimed at?

The cause of the disagreement
The way Sam assigns reviewers

items.prompt: What is a surface fix?

A fix applied only on the surface of a document
An instruction aimed at the visible behavior
items.explanation: It targets what can be seen, not what drives it.

items.prompt: Why did things go quiet for about a week?

The behavior eased while the cause stayed in place
Both had put the dispute behind them for good

items.prompt: What is a root cause here?

The most recent terse comment
The person who spoke first in review
items.explanation: Incidents are symptoms; the need underneath is the cause.

items.prompt: What often happens to the second flare-up after a failed fix?
choices: It is usually milder, because both are on notice now
It disappears once the rest of the team notices it
It tends to come back worse, since both feel unheard
items.explanation: The failed fix adds a second grievance to the original one.

'Please be nicer to each other in code review.'
'Let's find out together why reviews feel so tense.'

Yes, it proves a permanent gap in their personalities

items.explanation: Recurrence points at the fix, not at an unfixable pair.

Pick the engineer who is more correct
Help both name the real need
items.explanation: Addressing the need is what removes the reason for the behavior.

items.prompt: After a stern formal warning about review conduct, the clash between two engineers returns within a fortnight. Which reading best fits what happened?
choices: The warning pressed on behavior while the real disagreement stayed unidentified
The warning was too gentle, so a harsher one would finally end the clash for good
The two are incompatible, so reassigning one of them is the only real remedy
The warning worked, and the new clash is an unrelated second conflict between them
items.explanation: A stricter version of a surface fix is still a surface fix. Recurrence is the signal that the underlying disagreement was not found.

An interest, stated openly
items.explanation: It states a complaint, not the need behind it.

items.prompt: What is an interest?
choices: The reason behind what someone is asking for
The thing someone asks for, stated out loud
The outcome that the manager would prefer to see
items.explanation: Interest is the why; position is the what.

items.prompt: What does a neutral mediator do?
choices: Decides who is right and tells both of them so
Stays silent and lets the two of them settle it
Takes no side and proposes no solution up front
items.explanation: Neutral means structuring, not judging and not absent.

items.prompt: Which sentence is an interest?
choices: 'Stop leaving so many comments.'
'I need my judgment to be trusted.'
'Devon is being difficult.'
items.explanation: The first names a need; the others are demands or labels.

items.prompt: What is mediation?
choices: Helping two people resolve a conflict without picking a side
A manager ruling on which of two people is right
Two people each avoiding the other for a few weeks
items.explanation: The mediator facilitates; the two people resolve it.

items.prompt: What do people usually argue about?
choices: Interests
Root causes
Positions
items.explanation: The stated demands are what come up in the argument.

items.prompt: Can two opposed positions protect compatible interests?
choices: No, never
Yes, sometimes
Only when a manager decides
items.explanation: Different demands can protect needs that fit together.

items.prompt: What is a good first question to find an interest?
choices: 'What would it mean to you if that were true?'
'Who was the first one to start this dispute?'
'Can you both agree to calm down right now?'
items.explanation: It invites the reason behind the complaint.

items.prompt: An engineer says 'I want him to stop commenting on style.' Another says 'I want her to stop dismissing my review.' A manager treats these as the problem. What has been missed?
choices: Both are interests already, so nothing more needs to be asked of them
Both are demands, and the needs behind them were never asked about
The disagreement is only about which of them spoke up first
A written rule on comment style would settle it exactly as stated
items.explanation: Each sentence is a position. Interests only appear when someone asks what the demand protects.
items.reference:
Position versus interest
position: 'stop nitpicking'
interest: 'trust my judgment'
neutral: no side, no verdict
root cause: the need underneath
Why: people argue about positions, but the conflict is usually about the interests those positions protect.
items.learnMore:
Positions and interests

A position is the demand; an interest is the reason for the demand. Two demands that look opposed can protect compatible needs, which is why asking for the reason is the first mediator move.

Common mistake

Taking the position as the whole problem and negotiating only over it.
items.reflection: Recall a disagreement you had. What did you demand, and what were you actually protecting?

'Review requests should be answered within one working day or less'
items.explanation: Only the first names what the person is protecting. The others are demands or verdicts.

items.prompt: Priya's interest underneath 'he nitpicks' is that she wants what?
choices: Fewer review comments on all of her pull requests
A different reviewer assigned to each of her changes
Her design judgment to be trusted by her reviewers
items.explanation: The complaint hides a need to be seen as competent.

items.prompt: Devon's interest underneath 'she dismisses real issues' is that he wants what?
choices: Priya to be removed from the service
His careful review engaged with
More comments to be allowed
items.explanation: He wants his effort to count.

items.prompt: How do their two interests relate?
choices: They are near mirror images
They are directly opposed
They are unrelated
items.explanation: Each feels their competence is not respected.

items.prompt: Why are the positions 'nitpicky' and 'defensive' misleading?
choices: They are accurate descriptions of both
They are the only data a mediator needs
They sound opposed while the needs match
items.explanation: Labels hide the shared underlying need.

items.prompt: When does the symmetry become visible?
choices: Right after the first clash is noticed by the team
After each interest comes out in a separate talk
Only after a formal warning has been put on file
items.explanation: It takes separate conversations to see both needs.

items.prompt: What question reveals an interest behind a complaint?
choices: 'What does it mean to you when that is happening?'
'Why can't the two of you just get along better?'
'Which one of you is actually correct about this?'
items.explanation: It goes under the complaint instead of agreeing with it.

items.prompt: Is agreeing a coworker 'is rude' the same as asking what it feels like?
choices: Yes, both show support
Yes, both are neutral
No, agreeing takes a side first
items.explanation: Asking explores; agreeing concludes.

items.prompt: If both feel disrespected, the conflict is mostly about what?
choices: Who writes cleaner code overall
A shared need for respect of competence
Which written style guide the team has adopted this year
items.explanation: The need is the same even though the demands differ.

items.prompt: Two colleagues each say the other 'doesn't value my work.' A manager hears this and concludes they dislike each other. What reading fits better?
choices: They have incompatible standards that cannot be reconciled
One of them is likely exaggerating for effect
Each is describing the same unmet need from opposite sides
The statements cancel out and say nothing useful
items.explanation: Matching complaints are a clue to a shared need. Dislike is the visible layer.
items.reference:
Mirror-image interests
Priya: wants her judgment trusted
Devon: wants his review engaged with
both: feel competence unrespected
visible only after separate talks
Why: opposite-sounding positions can hide near-identical needs, and the symmetry only shows once each interest is surfaced.
items.learnMore:
Reading the symmetry

When both sides feel disrespected, the conflict is not 'nitpicky versus defensive' but a shared need being starved from both directions. Seeing that changes the conversation from blame to repair.

Common mistake

Assuming every conflict is a mirror image without checking.
items.reflection: Think of a standoff you were part of. Could the other person have been protecting the same need you were?

Compare the two written complaints for matching wording and phrasing
Assume symmetry and design the agreement around that assumption
Ask each person privately what the complaint would mean if true
items.explanation: The pattern is revealed by asking, not presumed. Private questions let each need appear unprompted.

It takes too long to say out loud in a meeting
It adopts one side's word as settled fact

No, a neutral mediator is active
Yes, but only at first
items.explanation: They structure and ask questions.

items.prompt: What does 'structural, not judicial' mean?
choices: Make room for interests, do not rule on positions
Rule quickly on the dispute so the matter is closed
Let whichever of the two is louder decide the outcome
items.explanation: The role is facilitation, not verdict.

items.prompt: What happens when a mediator signals agreement with one side?
choices: Both sides relax and begin to cooperate fully
The conflict ends once the manager has spoken up
The other side stops trusting the process
items.explanation: The other person sees two against one.

choices: It is always the wrong solution for the problem
Neither person did the work of understanding the other
It takes far too long for a manager to enforce
items.explanation: Understanding comes from doing the conversation, not receiving the result.

items.prompt: Does neutrality mean both people are equally right?
choices: No, it means not taking sides in the role
Yes, always, in every single claim they make
Yes, but only about the claims that were made first
items.explanation: It is about the mediator's stance, not a factual claim.

items.prompt: What can a neutral mediator do to keep the talk moving?
choices: Offer their own opinion on style
Wait for someone to give in
Ask questions that surface interests
items.explanation: Questions keep it from staying at the position level.

items.prompt: Midway through a conflict, a manager says to Priya in front of Devon: 'I understand your frustration with how Devon nitpicks.' Which neutrality problem is this?
choices: It proposes a solution before both of them have been heard
It asks Priya a question that is much too open for the setting
It names the interest before Priya had offered it herself
It repeats one side's framing as if it were agreed fact
items.explanation: The word 'nitpicks' belongs to Priya. Devon is likely to reject it before the real conversation begins.
items.reference:
What neutrality asks
no solution proposed first
no side's wording repeated as fact
active, not passive
structural, not judicial
Why: the mediator makes room for interests to surface; deciding whose position wins is what ends the trust.
items.learnMore:
Neutral is not passive

Neutrality is a set of behaviors: ask, structure, and withhold verdicts. A mediator who stays out of the way leaves the talk at the position level, which is a failure of the role.

Common mistake

Treating neutral as silent and expecting the two to sort it out unaided.
items.reflection: When you have mediated or been mediated, what small signal showed whose side the helper was on?

Step back and let the two resolve it without any prompting at all
items.explanation: Neutrality is a discipline: the view may exist, but voicing it converts the mediator into a judge.

Yes, right away and in full detail

items.prompt: A manager schedules a joint meeting at once, saying open conversation is best. What is the most likely outcome?
choices: Each person defends their own position in front of the other
Each person names their deeper interest out loud to the other
The disagreement dissolves once the two simply sit together
The manager learns both interests before anyone has spoken
items.explanation: Without private space, the real interests are rarely volunteered cold, so the position-level argument repeats.
items.reference:
Stage 1: separate conversations
Sam meets Priya alone
Sam meets Devon alone
ask: what would it mean if true?
interest appears: 'he doesn't think I know what I'm doing'
Why: people rarely state a real interest cold in front of the other person, so private space comes first.
items.learnMore:
Why private first

A private conversation lets someone say what they would not say with the other person listening. It is for hearing interests, not for collecting ammunition against anyone.

Common mistake

Going straight to a joint meeting, which usually replays the argument with an audience.

items.prompt: A joint session begins with 'let's go through the disputed comments one by one.' Why is this a risky structure?

It keeps the talk at the position level, where the fight repeats
It skips the stage in which Sam announces the final decision
It pushes back the date of the follow-up check-in by a week
items.explanation: Re-litigating comments is the position-level fight. The structure should ask for how it feels, not what happened.

'Talk it out' tends to restart the argument. A structure, one speaks about how it feels while the other only listens, forces the shift from position to interest.

Pause the interruption and ask them to hold it until their turn
End the session and then meet them separately once more again

items.learnMore:
Structure over free talk

'Talk it out' tends to restart the argument. A structure, one speaks about how it feels while the other only listens, forces the shift from position to interest.

Common mistake

Letting the joint talk drift back into re-arguing which comments were fair.

items.prompt: Is every conflict a mirror image?
choices: No, not always
Yes, always
Yes, in a team of two people
items.explanation: Some have one legitimate side.

items.prompt: What if Devon's comments were mostly personal style preference?
choices: The mirror-image approach still fits exactly
The conflict has no cause
The conflict may be one-sided in substance
items.explanation: Then Priya's pushback might be reasonable.

items.prompt: Who finds out which shape the conflict has?
choices: The manager's first impression of the two people
The process itself, via the mediator's questions
Whichever of the two argues loudest in the room
items.explanation: Shape is discovered, not assumed.

items.prompt: What can go wrong with assuming symmetry?
choices: A legitimate grievance goes unaddressed
The meeting ends up running a little too short
Nobody ends up willing to speak at all in the room
items.explanation: Treating it as a misunderstanding hides a real issue.

items.prompt: Can a mediator still be neutral when one side is plainly reasonable?
choices: No, they must then quietly pick a side in the end
No, because mediation can then never be used again
Yes, by addressing the problem directly and fairly
items.explanation: Neutrality is about process, not hiding a real issue.

items.prompt: What is this unit's worked example, a case or the whole territory?
choices: The whole territory
One case among many
A rule for every team
items.explanation: It is a case to extend.

items.prompt: If only one person will join a joint session, what then?
choices: The method needs adapting
Nothing needs to change
The matter is closed
items.explanation: The structure assumes both take part.

items.prompt: Sam's private talks show Devon's comments were mostly style preferences and Priya's pushback was reasonable. What does this change?
choices: It proves that the earlier mirror-image finding was right after all
It means that the joint session should now be skipped entirely
It means Sam should now quietly side with Priya in private
It points to a one-sided problem to address directly, not a mutual misunderstanding
items.explanation: The process revealed an asymmetric case. Forcing a symmetric story would leave the real problem untouched.

items.learnMore:
One case, not the territory

Separate talks followed by a structured joint session is a reusable method. The mirror-image result belongs to this case only; some conflicts have a legitimate grievance on one side that needs direct attention.

Common mistake

Treating a real one-directional problem as a mutual misunderstanding.
items.reflection: Think of a conflict where one side was genuinely in the wrong. What would 'finding the shared need' have hidden?

The manager cannot claim neutrality and holds power over the outcome
The structure only works between people of a similar age
The manager's own interests are never relevant to the matter
